answer.label: Not Thomas Jefferson — actually Coleman Cox
answer.authorDates: Early-20th-century American epigrammatist · coined the line by 1922
answer.sourceLine: This is a spurious Jefferson quotation. The adage was crafted by San Francisco aphorist Coleman Cox and printed in his 1922 booklet “Listen to This” as “I am a great believer in luck. The harder I work, the more of it I seem to have.” It was not attached to Thomas Jefferson until 1977, and it appears nowhere in his writings.

source.heading: Where it really comes from
source.excerpt: I am a great believer in luck. The harder I work, the more of it I seem to have.
trail: The earliest known appearance is in Coleman Cox’s 1922 collection “Listen to This,” and Cox was credited by name in the January 1923 Colorado School of Mines Magazine, per Quote Investigator.

The Thomas Jefferson credit first surfaces in Laurence J. Peter’s 1977 compendium Peter’s Quotations: Ideas for Our Time — more than a century after Jefferson’s death and half a century after Cox coined the line (Quote Investigator).
Monticello’s Jefferson Encyclopedia lists it as a spurious quotation, noting it has never been found in Jefferson’s papers.
Over the years the same line has also been floated to Stephen Leacock (1955) and Samuel Goldwyn (1976 biography) — a classic sign of a free-floating aphorism, per Quote Investigator.
source.excerptNote: Coleman Cox’s original 1922 wording. The smoother modern form — “I’m a great believer in luck, and I find the harder I work the more I have of it” — is the version later mis-stamped with Jefferson’s name.

source.rightsNote: The saying was first published in Coleman Cox’s booklet “Listen to This” (1922). A work published in the United States before 1931 is in the public domain, so the wording itself is free to use — but it should not be credited to Thomas Jefferson.

author.name: Coleman Cox
author.heading: Who was Coleman Cox?
author.metaLine: Early-20th-century American epigrammatist and businessman, San Francisco
author.bio: Coleman Cox was an American businessman and epigrammatist active in the early 20th century, known for self-published booklets of pithy maxims. His 1922 collection Listen to This is the earliest documented home of this now-famous line about luck and hard work. As the aphorism spread, his name fell away and grander figures — Jefferson, Leacock, Goldwyn — were substituted in his place.

misattribution.heading: How Jefferson got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s classic “Jefferson said it” quotations — feel-good, clever, and completely undocumented in his writings. The real trail is short and modern.

items.why: Jefferson (1743–1826) died nearly a century before the phrase was coined. Monticello lists it as a spurious quotation, and it appears in none of his papers; the credit first shows up in Laurence J. Peter’s 1977 Peter’s Quotations, per Quote Investigator.
A 1955 Louisiana newspaper pinned a version of the saying on the Canadian humorist — decades after Cox’s original, per Quote Investigator.
A 1976 biography linked the words to the movie producer without claiming he coined them, per Quote Investigator.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented source is Coleman Cox’s 1922 booklet Listen to This; every famous-name version came later, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why the line sticks
lead: The appeal is the paradox: luck sounds like something that happens to you, yet the punchline hands the credit back to effort. That neat reversal is exactly the kind of self-made-success wisdom that gets pinned on Founding Fathers and moguls to borrow their authority.

In reality it belongs to a jobbing aphorist, Coleman Cox, whose 1922 maxim was clean enough to outlive his name. The idea itself is older still — the proverb “Diligence is the mother of good luck” runs back centuries — but the memorable modern wording is Cox’s.
context.pull: Luck sounds like something that happens to you — the line hands the credit back to work.
